Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 1:

(p-21) The purpose of Surat al-Fajr

Its purpose is to establish, by evidence, the return (al-iyab) and the reckoning (al-hisab) mentioned at the end of Surat al-Ghashiyah. The most indicative of this purpose in it is the dawn (al-fajr), by the breaking forth of morning from the day that passed yesterday without any difference in its essence, and by the rising of those who slept from the lesser death, which is sleep, spreading out to seek livelihood, [all of this pointing] to the requital in the reckoning, with reward and punishment.

"In the name of Allah" (bismillah): the One who gathers the servants after they have been scattered, by the greatness that is His.

"The Most Merciful" (al-Rahman): the One who encompassed them with mercy after the generality of creation through bringing into existence, with the clarifying [revelation] that prepares whoever He wills for faith.

"The Most Merciful" (al-Rahim): the One who singled out His friends with good pleasure, which makes Paradise lawful [for them].

* *

When that surah concluded by stating that there must be a return and a reckoning, and since the alternation of night and day, and the renewal of each of them after its annihilation, is a sign of the power to resurrect, and since Allah had made the Hajj in His law, in the manner of being stripped of sewn garments, the obligation of the talbiyah, and travel to the specified places, a sign reminding of that, He said: ﴿By the dawn﴾, i.e., the perfect one in this attribute, by reason of its greatness, so that it is as if there were no dawn other than it. It is the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), which is the first of the days that begin the return to the House of Allah, the Sacred House, by entering its sanctuary, being released from its prohibitions, and eating of its hospitality.

When he mentioned this day, with the expression used for it being more indicative of resurrection, because it bursts forth from a dawn that has already shone and a day that has been completed and ended, with no distinction between it and what has passed, he generalized, saying, expressing by the opposite: ﴿And ten nights﴾, which are the greatest nights of the year. And they are a sign of God upon resurrection, by rising to answer the summons of God Most High in the manner of the dead.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 3:

﴿Wal-shaf'i﴾, i.e., for one who hastens in two days; ﴿wal-watri﴾, i.e., for one who completes. This was said by Ibn al-Zubayr. Ahmad and al-Bazzar, with men who are those of the Sahih, related from ʿAyyash ibn ʿUqba, who is trustworthy, from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The ten nights are the ten of al-Adha, the even (shaf') is the Day of al-Adha, and the odd (watr) is the Day of ʿArafa."

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 4:**

Since the alternation of the night and the day is more indicative of power and more manifest as a blessing, He said, returning the last of the oath to its first part and reminding of the blessing and the perfection of power: because the night hides them both by journeying and by secret travel, it is greater than them both in that matter, since the travel of the day is apparent due to its illumination, unlike the night, which is hidden by its alteration, and so it was more indicative of power. ﴿By the night﴾, that is, of the night of departure (*nafar*), ﴿when it passes﴾, that is, when it ends, as the night of this world and the darkness of its wrongs end, and dawn succeeds it, and those who have returned to God, returning to their homes after laying down their burdens, travel in it. [And the last of the oath has returned to its first part.] Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub affirmed the *ya'* in *yasri*, while the rest omitted it. The reason for its omission was asked about by al-Mu'arrij al-Akhfash, who said: "Serve me for a year." He asked him again after a year, and he said: "The night is traversed in it, and it does not traverse." He thus diverted it from its meaning, so it was necessary that he divert from its wording, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾ [Maryam: 28], for when he diverted from *bāghiyah* (unchaste), its wording was diverted, so he did not say *bughyah* (unchastity). This is the end of the quotation, and it returns to the wording, although it entails rejecting the narrations of affirmation. The spiritual wisdom in it, and God knows best, pertains to the one who travels and to what the travel takes place in. As for the one who travels, it is their division on the night of departure into one who stays and one who returns to his land. So the ones who stay are alluded to by the omission, as an encouragement to that, because of the majesty of the paths in it; thus the night of their union was not entirely ended, and they seize its arrival and delight in its length in those sites, sensations and places of worship. And the ones who return are alluded to by the affirmation, because the night has passed entirely from them; they have returned to their homes in what has been uncovered of their day. As for what the travel takes place in, it indicates its length at times and its brevity at others. The omission indicates the short [and] the affirmation indicates the long, by what occurred of the completion of its journey, and what occurred to the travellers in it of standing in the presence of the Ancient Attribute before the All-Knowing King, as the Imam Taqi al-Din ibn Daqiq al-'Id, may Allah have mercy on him, said, alluding to that:

> *How many a night in You we have traversed by night,*
> *Knowing neither closing of the eyes nor rest.*

The verses attributed to him are in *al-Muzzammil*. The night has thus been divided into the long and the short, and the traveller in it into the one present and the one on a journey. The variation in that, and in all the instances of the oath, indicates that its Doer is a Single, Choosing, Subduing Power. For this reason He followed the indication with the subjugation of the subduers and the destruction of the tyrants. As for *baghiyy* (unchaste), its wisdom has been mentioned in Maryam.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 89, verse 5:

Since this is a great oath, mentioning those nights which include the remembrance of those sacred places and what occurs in them of gatherings and weeping, as Abu Talib said in his famous rhymed *lamiyya* ode:

؎Night of Jam' and the abodes in Mina,
∗∗∗ and is there above them any sanctity or abodes?

And since it reminds of the Resurrection and points to it with a clear rational proof, namely the bringing into existence after non-existence, together with the grandeur these things have in themselves and in the hearts of those addressed by them, Allah the Glorified and Exalted drew attention to this by His saying: ﴿Is there in that﴾, that is, in what has been mentioned, along with its lofty matter and manifest worth, ﴿an oath﴾, that is, a sufficient and convincing one, ﴿for one of understanding﴾, that is, the possessor of ﴿ḥijr﴾ (intellect, restraint), who restrains him and keeps him from desire in the grasp of desire, so that it raises him to the summit of guidance, in the ascent of exaltation, until he knows that the One who did what this oath includes will not leave him neglected, and that He is able to give life to the dead. Ibn Jarir said: It is said of a man who is master of himself, subduing it and controlling it, that he is truly *dhū ḥijr* [the possessor of ḥijr]. [End of quotation. So whoever reaches the point where his intellect restrains him from sins and carries him to noble deeds, he is *dhū ḥijr*.]

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Allah the Glorified began, for those previously mentioned, another aspect of consideration, which is that they should remember the condition of those nations who came before them and what their denial and transgression brought upon them. So He said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?﴾ [Al-Fajr: 6], up to His saying: ﴿Iram of the pillars?﴾ [Al-Fajr: 7], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [Al-Fajr: 14], that is, nothing of the transgressions of creatures is hidden from Him, and nothing that they conceal escapes Him: ﴿It is the same whether one of you conceals speech or speaks it aloud﴾ [Al-Ra'd: 10]. Why, then, would these people not take heed from what they see and witness of the creation of camels, the raising of the sky, the setting up of mountains, and the spreading of the earth? All of this is for their benefit and advantage: the camels for their burdens and travel, the sky for their watering and shade, the mountains for storing their water and their provisions, and the earth for their settling and their journeys. Yet they have gained no insight through all these matters, nor have they taken lessons from those generations that passed away.

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd?﴾ [Al-Fajr: 6], despite the great extent of their rebellion and the pure falsehood of their slander, ﴿Indeed, your Lord is ever watchful﴾ [Al-Fajr: 14]. Then they will remember at a time when remembrance will not benefit them: ﴿when the earth is leveled, pounded to powder﴾ [Al-Fajr: 21], ﴿and your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [Al-Fajr: 22], ﴿and Hell is brought near that Day﴾ [Al-Fajr: 23], ﴿that Day man will remember, but how will the remembrance benefit him?﴾ [Al-Fajr: 23]. [End.]

Given that the intended sense, as the context indicates, is: "They will all be raised up humbled, then they will be gathered, then they will be called to account, and each person will be recompensed for what he did. So if they believe in that, they will be saved; otherwise, the One whose power over the greatest punishment is established after the lesser punishment will punish them, by reason of His power over resurrection, by reason of His power over what you have seen of the creation of camels, the sky, the mountains and the earth, with the wonders in each of them, by reason of His power over everything." This is the principal intended meaning, and the omission (ḥadhf) of further elaboration serves to magnify it, relying on the audience's knowledge of what the context has indicated throughout the surah and what precedes it. Since He omitted the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam, the completion of the oath's statement) to direct the reader to what the context guides toward and to make the meaning rest on it, and to create awe, while knowing that an oath has no sense without something sworn to, and since the power to do it had already been indicated by the thing sworn by, He clarified that power through the matter of the lesser punishment for the earlier nations. So He said, addressing the one who was told at the end of that ﴿So remind, for you are only a reminder﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 21], as consolation to him (ﷺ) and as an indication that no one else can truly reflect on it as it deserves, and as a threat to those among his people who denied:

﴿Have you not seen﴾, meaning: look with the eye of reflection, O most noble of Our messengers, so that you may know with a knowledge that is, in its certainty, like what is perceived by sight. He expressed this by way of a question to indicate that what he urged him to see is worthy of being asked about: ﴿how your Lord dealt﴾, meaning: the One who has favored you by sending you as the seal of all the prophets, with the earlier nations, for what they shared with these people in denying the messengers and in making the object of their concern this world, and in acting as those who think they will live forever. He began with the most severe of them in that and the most insolent, those who said: "Who is stronger than us in power?" So He said: ﴿ʿĀd﴾, meaning: those who went to such extremes of severity that they said: "Who is stronger than us in power?" Their prophet Hud (ﷺ) said to them: ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you will abide forever﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 129]. Their building of a garden in this worldly life, which is the abode of passing away, of departure and removal, of hardship, trial and turbidity, of sickness, misery and harm, indicates this. Then He said, clarifying for them, with an elided mudāf (a omitted noun governing the construction):

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 7:

﴿Iram﴾ means its people and its chief men. The name is applied to them because of the very close association with what it contained of wondrous building and remarkable distinction. Then he clarified it by his saying: ﴿of the pillars﴾, meaning possessing the lofty building that is firm upon pillars, the like of which was not present in this world; and for this reason he said:

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 8:**

﴿Which had not been created﴾, meaning: which no one has the power to make or build. The verb is in the passive form to indicate generality. ﴿The like of it﴾: the pronoun may refer to *'Ad* by way of the tribe, or to *Iram* by way of the city. He clarifies this by generalizing to the whole earth, saying: ﴿in the lands﴾, meaning in their construction, their amenities (p. 28), their fruits, the distribution of their waters and rivers, the goodness of their soil, the beauty of their birds, and all that gathered there, which exceeds counting and defeats the powers. Nor was there a like of its people who built it in the strength of their bodies, the greatness of their station, and their other affairs. Its owner was Shaddad, who ruled the entire inhabited world, and so he took it as his domain and built it in a desert of Aden over three hundred years, seeking to rival Paradise by it, as he claimed. These are hearts that went astray and led others astray, and the Creator of them led them astray. Abu Hayyan said: its attributes are far-fetched, or practically impossible, that there should be anything like it on earth. When it was completed as he intended, he set out to dwell in it, and he was then nine hundred years old. When he was at a distance of one day and night from it, Allah sent upon them a blast from the sky, and it destroyed them, so they became like yesterday that has gone. He concealed their city, and no one saw it except Abdullah ibn Qilaba. He went out in search of camels that had strayed from him in the time of Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, and he came upon it. When he left it and separated from it, it became hidden from him. He had carried with him some of what he had seen there of pearls, musk and saffron, and he sold it. Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, heard of this and sent for him, and he related the account to him. [Then he sent,] Mu'awiyah, may Allah be pleased with him, to Ka'b al-Ahbar and asked him about that. He said: it is Iram of the pillars, and a man from among the Muslims will enter it in your time, reddish-white, short, with a mole on his eyebrows and a mole on his heel, who goes out in search of a camel of his. Then (p. 29) he turned and saw Ibn Qilaba and said: this, by Allah, is that man. Our shaykh mentioned this in the takhrij of the hadiths of al-Kashshaf [and] said: traces of fabrication are apparent in it. A group of scholars, among them Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: all these attributes belong to the tribe, namely the first 'Ad, and its name Iram is after their forefather. They were nomadic Arabs who built their houses on pillars, according to the custom of the Arabs. Allah did not create the like of them as a nation among the nations in all the lands.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 9:

When he began with these (the 'Ad), because their affair was more astonishing and their story more remarkable and strange, he followed with the nation closest to them in time and most similar to them in condition, because they were made affluent with what they were given of gardens, springs, crops and palm trees whose spathes are soft and bending (هَضِيم, hadim: tender, easily broken). So they put in the place of the gratitude that was incumbent upon them ingratitude (kufr), and they preferred blindness (al-'ama) over guidance (al-huda), despite what was in their sign, which is the she-camel, of great indication of power. So he said: ﴿And Thamud, who hewed out the rocks in the valley﴾, i.e., they dug out and cut out, cutting in a real sense, as if for them it was a matter of obligation; ﴿the rocks in the valley﴾, i.e., [the valley of] al-Hijr or the Valley of the Villages (Wadi al-Qura). They made houses hewn into the mountains, acting like one who would overcome time and bring the age to an end. Abu Hayyan said: It is said that the first to carve mountains, rocks and marble was Thamud, and they built one thousand and seven hundred cities (p-30), all of them of stone.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 10:

When he (Allah) had mentioned the two tribes of the Arabs, He mentioned [some of] those tyrants of the non-Arabs (ʿAjam) who were their neighbours, because of what their story contains of arrogance and tyranny, together with the strange events and extraordinary wonders it holds, especially in regard to the power to resurrect (al-baʿth) through the turning of the staff into a serpent and its returning to inanimate wood again, repeatedly, and through the bringing forth of frogs and lice from the heaps of the earth, and other things. So He said: ﴿And Pharaoh﴾, meaning, and He dealt with Pharaoh ﴿of the stakes﴾, meaning the one who fixed his kingdom firmly, in the manner of one who thinks it will not be removed by armies, troops and others, and by everything he thought would strengthen his affair, such as gardens, springs, crops and noble dwellings. So the outstretched hand became his in the kingdom.

Since what is meant by Pharaoh is he and his soldiers, because the head is used as a figurative expression (kināya, metonymy) for the body, as it is the group and the means of its existence, he described him with an attribute that encompasses his people and all who are mentioned here, so he said: ﴿Those who﴾ meaning Pharaoh and his soldiers and every disbeliever mentioned here, from ʿĀd and Thamūd and their followers, ﴿transgressed﴾ meaning they went beyond the limits, ﴿in the lands﴾ meaning [which] they actually possessed and others that they held by potential.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 12:

﴿Then they multiplied corruption therein﴾ following their transgression and because of it, ﴿therein﴾ through what they did of disbelief and wrongdoing, which became a precedent for whoever heard of it.

(When that was what required the punishment, He made His saying the consequence of it: ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a whip of punishment﴾), that is, sent down (إنزالًا, inzal) of the utmost force ﴿upon them﴾, that is, in this world, ﴿your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you (المُحْسِن, al-muhsin), who manages your affair (المُدَبِّر لِأمْرِكَ), who made the reports of past nations and the traces of the sects a foundation (مَوْطِئًا, mawti') for them ﴿a whip of punishment﴾, that is, He made their punishment, by drowning, by the quake, and other means, at its time, its firm establishment, its height and its encompassing, like something poured out in the severity of its striking, its adhesion to the one struck, its swiftness toward him, and its wrapping around him, like the whip (السَّوْط, sawt). In its being of diverse kinds, interlacing into varieties, the root of it is mixing (الخَلْط, al-khalt). This braided lash with which one is struck was named so because its strands are mixed with one another, and because it mixes flesh and blood. It has also been said: what befell them in this world was likened to a whip, to indicate repetition and recurrence until the one punished by it perishes, and to announce that, compared with what He prepared for them in the Hereafter, it is like a whip compared with a sword: "This is the whip of the world, and the sword of the Hereafter is sharper, keener and more piercing." Then he gave the reason for His seizing every wrongdoer and His vengeance upon every corrupter, saying that He is watchful (رَقِيب, raqib), and he spoke in an emphatic manner, depicting that the sinners cannot escape Him, as an alert to the fact that the deeds of those who deny this, or who do not think of it, are [recorded and known]:

﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾, i.e., your Master, who manages the affair of your prophethood, ﴿is ever watchful﴾, i.e., nothing escapes Him. Rather, He is capable of everything and has knowledge of everything, the knowledge of one who intends to remain in a place of observation (المِرْصاد, *al-mirsad*) at its appointed time, with the utmost preservation and watchfulness. He is capable of whatever He wills. (p-٣٢)

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned that the customary conduct of these groups was ṭughyān (insolence and transgression), and mentioned that the customary way of the Lord, glory be to Him, toward those who turn away and disbelieve is that He punishes them [as] He threatened at the end of that, and He indicated this by what had been witnessed among the nations, and gave the reason for it, namely that He is not heedless, [He mentioned] the general custom of man, insofar as he is man, without restricting it to these groups, regarding being tested in states of ease and hardship. So He said, alluding to the answer to what the disbelievers used to say, that they are more favoured by God than the Muslims and that He does not help them in this world, and that the Companions, may God be pleased with them, reduce their share of this world. This is a consequence of what has passed, linked to what is implied, as if to say: this was the custom of these nations and the custom of God regarding them. ﴿As for man﴾, that is, the one whom He placed in the womb so that he might reason about these oaths and what is intended from him, namely belief in what the one who swears by them is asserting, and who was created inclined to forgetfulness, to attachment to himself, to love of this world, and to contentment with it.

Since the aim was to describe his condition at the beginning, He placed the adverbial phrase indicating this before the predicate, and so He said: ﴿when﴾, and He emphasised the matter with the negative, so He said: ﴿his Lord tests him not﴾. That is, He treats him as one being examined, by mixing with him what He wills of a mixing that inclines him and changes him, ﴿his Lord﴾, that is, the One who originated him and dealt kindly with him by what preserves his existence, so that his gratitude or ingratitude may become manifest (p-33). ﴿Then honours him﴾, that is, by making him esteemed [among people] and giving him what they honour him with, of rank and wealth. ﴿And bestows favour upon him﴾, that is, by making him one who enjoys pleasures and luxury through what He has given him, [without fatigue] because of it. ﴿Then he says﴾, out of joy at that and boastfulness: ﴿My Lord has honoured me﴾, that is, the One who brought me into being and manages my affairs. He thinks that this is by right, and so he becomes elated by it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 16:

﴿Wa-amma﴾ is here in the sense of ﴿idhā﴾ (when), and he emphasized the pattern of the first [verse], so he said: ﴿Mā ibtalāhu﴾, i.e., his Lord tested him, in order to make manifest his patience or his impatience.

Since his saying in the first [verse], "Then He honored him and bestowed favors upon him," was a metonymy (kināya) for "Then He expanded [his provision] for him," he contrasted it here with his saying: ﴿Fa-qadara﴾, i.e., He constricted, the constriction of one who manages a matter with reckoning and measure, ﴿'alayhi rizqahu﴾ (upon him his provision). So it is a metonymy for constriction, just as giving without reckoning is a metonymy for abundance. He made it [the provision] in the measure of his necessity, without which a person ordinarily cannot live, and did not give him anything beyond that. He did not say "Then He humiliated him" in place of "He measured upon him," as a teaching of good manners toward Him, glorified and exalted is He, and as a safeguarding of the people of God from this expression, because most of them are constricted in their worldly life; and because withholding honor is not confined to being humiliation. ﴿Fa-yaqūlu﴾, i.e., the human being [because of the constriction] (p-34): ﴿Rabbī﴾, i.e., the one who nurtures me, ﴿ahānan﴾ (has humiliated me). So he is preoccupied with that, is distressed by it, and this becomes his greatest concern.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 17:

Since attributing this [treatment] to Him would be a rebuke and a reproach for the shortness of his vision, for restriction of provision may lead to the happiness of both abodes, while abundance may lead to the wretchedness of both, and this is what is most commonly found, He said, as a deterrent from this kind of statement, with the strongest instruments of restraint, giving the reason for expansion and restriction: ﴿No!﴾ [That is,] I do not honour by increasing worldly goods, nor do I humiliate by decreasing them. Expansion is not confined to honour, nor is constriction confined to humiliation and abasement. Humiliation comes to them only because they do not obey God. Sometimes [a person is tested] with expansion and sometimes with restriction. Sometimes a person disobeys and He expands [his provision] for him as a humiliation to him; this is for the one whom He wills wretchedness, so He hastens his good things in this world as a gradual lure (istidraj). And sometimes a person disobeys and He restricts [his provision] for him as an honour [to him], because that expiates his sins for him. In the Sahih, the hadith of the bald man, the leper and the blind man among the Children of Israel is a great witness to this.

When He had forbidden the belief that expansion is for the honoured and restriction for the humiliated, He mentioned that the criterion for one who is created with love of obedience, and for one who is created with [love of] disobedience, is hatred and love of this world. So He said, [expressing] about human speech in both cases (p-35), [the singular] first because it is more explicit in generality, and [the plural] second to inform that the intended meaning is the genus: ﴿Nay﴾, that is, they make light of God's command because of the disobedience they have, so He expands [provision] for some of those created for wretchedness, as a humiliation to them through gradual lure, and restricts [provision] for some of those not created for that, as an honour to them and as a deterrent from following desire and a return to kindness toward the weak. He expressed this disobedience, which is the cause of abandonment, by His saying: ﴿you do not honour the orphan﴾, that is, most people do not [honour] ﴿the orphan﴾ by giving and the like, out of compassion for him and mercy toward him, because he is weak and no benefit is hoped for from him, either by praise or otherwise.

Since a person is prevented from urging others to good only by love of this world, if the one being urged is greater than him, he saves it for his own needs; and if he is his equal, he fears that he will be repaid in kind by it, so he urges him to feed another poor man. Urging others to give (al-ihsan bil-hath 'ala al-i'ta') is greater than giving itself, because giving necessarily follows from it, unlike the reverse. He says: ﴿And you do not urge one another﴾, meaning, they do not urge, with a great urging, their own families or others, ﴿to feed the poor﴾, meaning, to give generously to him out of bounty and munificence. Thus, its ascription to him (the poor) is an indication that he is a partner of the wealthy in his wealth to the extent of the zakat.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 19:

(p-36) When he indicated the love of the world by an external matter, he indicated it by a matter within man, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And you devour﴾, meaning in a manner of renewal and continuity, ﴿the inheritance﴾, that is, the legacy (al-mirath). Its root is wirath, and the waw was replaced by a ta'. It is as if He expressed it by this form to indicate the taking of the outward aspect, which the waw points to, and the searching for the inward aspect, which is indicated by the articulation point of the ta', a searching that perhaps leads to taking part of the property of others: ﴿greedily devouring﴾, that is, with lamm (gathering and mixing), meaning mixing together what is lawful and what is unlawful. For they did not bequeath to women or to children, and they would devour what the heir had gathered, even though they knew it was unlawful, and they would say: "None deserves the wealth except one who fights and protects the territory."

When this [i.e., the mistreatment of orphans and neglect of the poor] is done out of necessity [yet with aversion], He says something that is explicit about the intended meaning: ﴿and you love wealth﴾, i.e., continually, ﴿this kind of wealth, whatever it may be﴾, and He emphasizes it with the verbal noun and the adjective, saying: ﴿with an abundant love﴾, i.e., much, with greed and avarice. Thus their ultimate concern became worldly consideration, and they did not turn their souls away from their love of it toward what the intellect calls for, which restrains the soul from desire, the restraint that holds it back from base pleasures, and the discernment that forbids it from appetites, toward turning to Allah.

(p-37) Since the context points to the implied meaning: "They think that this will increase their wealth, improve their circumstances, and relieve their anxiety," He restrained them with the most comprehensive form of restraint, saying: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning: the matter should not be this way. Then he resumed by mentioning what necessitates their regret, awakens them from their slumber, and informs them that the love of wealth does not necessitate its growth; and even if it did necessitate its growth, that would not necessitate its being a cause of happiness. So He said: ﴿When the earth is crushed﴾, meaning: its crushing, shaking and quaking occurs in order to level it, so that it becomes like a hide stretched out by intense pulling, with no crookedness in it in any way. By using the passive form (al-bina' lil-maf'ul) He indicated the ease of this, because the matter is great owing to the greatness of the True Agent. For this reason He said: ﴿crushed, crushed﴾, meaning: repeatedly, distributed over every place within it that is raised, so that every mountain, hill, mound and pass has a crushing specific to it, individually, in order to convey that it is a thorough crushing; thus its mountains and hills become scattered dust, and then it levels out so that nothing of crookedness remains in it. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for tremendous earthquakes which the firm mountains cannot bear, so that they are reduced to other than themselves.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 22:

When the leveling indicated the coming of a great matter, for it is the custom in this world that roads are not swept, sprinkled, or leveled in their entirety except for the arrival of a great personage such as a sultan, he spoke, showing gentleness to the addressee from the end of Surat al-Buruj until here, by mentioning the attribute of beneficence in a manner that shatters the livers of his opponents: ﴿And your Lord has come﴾, that is, the command of the One who has shown kindness to you, by displaying your supreme exaltation on that greatest day, for the decisive judgment among the servants (p-38) through your intercession. ﴿And the angel﴾, that is, this category, with the angels being arrayed ﴿rank upon rank﴾, that is, their arrangement being distributed according to their kinds, each kind a rank of its own. They encircle the people of the lowest heaven with the jinn and humankind, and the people of every heaven likewise, and they are double in number those who have surrounded him, until they encircle the people of the seventh heaven, all of them, and they are double in number all the creatures who have surrounded him.

The meaning of his coming, glorified and exalted is He, after we negate that it resembles the coming of any created thing, is that He, glorified and exalted is He, "there is nothing like unto Him" (Qur'an 42:11) in His essence, His attributes, or His acts. So when we affirm this creed in all that belongs to the ambiguous verses (mutashabih), we say that in this case it is like His command, glorified and exalted is He, in the manifestation of the signs of His power and the clarification of the traces of His might, dominion and authority. When a king comes in person, the manifestation of the awe and governance that appears by his presence is something that does not appear through the appearance of all his armies without him. So his coming is an expression of his rule, the display of his greatness and his might, and all that kings display when they come to a place. He, glorified and exalted is His state, is present with those who are judged among them by His knowledge and power. He is never described as absent, neither from eternity nor to eternity. So His presence in [that] state and His distance as before that, without any difference at all, and nothing new has occurred (p-39) except the linking of His power, according to His will, to the separating of creation. Had He been absent at a time, or had His absence been possible such that He would need to come, He would be needy; and had He been needy, He would be incapable; and had He been incapable, or had incapacity been possible for Him in any state, He would not be fit for divinity. Exalted is Allah far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say, a great exaltation.

The repetition of “صَفًّا” (ṣaffan) is an alert to turning the "coming" away from its literal sense, and a guidance toward what I mentioned of the analogy (tamthil).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 23:

Since Hell (jahannam) does not come by itself, for if it came by itself, one might suppose that it had escaped from [God's] power; rather, the angels lead it. So whenever they strive with it, going and returning, there befalls the people from that such terror as none knows except Allah the Exalted. And the object of terror was the very act of bringing it, not the identity of those who do it; therefore the verb ﴿wujiʾa﴾ (it is brought) is put in the passive form. That is, with the easiest of matters, ﴿on that Day﴾, that is, when what was mentioned has occurred, ﴿Hell (jahannam)﴾, that is, the Fire which scowls upon those who burn in it. It has been related that "it will be brought with seventy thousand reins, and with each rein seventy thousand angels." This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Hell will be made manifest to whoever sees﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 36]. And ﴿on that Day﴾ is substituted for "idha" (when) as an explanation, because of the length of the separation, and as an intensification of the terror. That is, when these matters have occurred, ﴿man will see what has been prepared for the grateful and what has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾.

Since He placed these magnificent matters and awful, terrifying calamities first, out of concern for them and as an alert that they, because of their great admonition, deserve that every hearer be admonished by them, He mentioned the agent of its time-adverb and changed it, saying: ﴿Man will remember (yatadhakkaru al-insan)﴾, that is, in a manner of renewal and continuity, so he will recall everything that was beneficial to him in the world and what harmed him, and he will know that his love of the world brought him nothing but loss; it added nothing to him of what was not written for him, nor did spending it diminish anything of what was written for him or what he spent. When he remembers this, spending becomes easy for him. And that abode is not the abode of action; therefore He said: ﴿But how (wa-anna) will remembrance (al-dhikra) be for him?﴾, that is, how and in what way will the great benefit of remembrance be his? For it is in a place other than its own, so it benefits him not at all in any way, because the abode of action has passed; and it yields nothing but regret and the multiplication of grief, sorrow and pains.

Since regret calls for a person to do what contradicts it, he explains that there is no action except the display of regret. So he resumes his speech: ﴿He will say﴾, that is, wishing for the impossible in a manner of renewal and continuity: ﴿"Oh, if only I had sent ahead"﴾ — and does "law" (لَيْتَ, "if only") benefit anything? — ﴿"for my life"﴾, that is, I would have made advance provision for what would benefit me of earnestness and action in it, ﴿"for my life"﴾, that is, during the days of my life in this world, or for the sake of this lasting life after which there is no death. It is possible that the reason for this wish of his is his knowledge that he was free in the world, and that acts of obedience in themselves were possible for him, with no apparent barrier preventing him from them (p-41) except diverting his soul away from them and his not applying to them the powers that God had given him.

Since this (i.e., his regret) would not benefit him, the next statement is connected to it: ﴿So on that Day﴾, that is, when all these matters have occurred, ﴿none will punish﴾, that is, none will inflict ﴿His punishment﴾, that is, the punishment of [God, that is,] its like of His absolute, unqualified punishment, so how much more so His chastisement. And since the longing to know the agent was intense, He brought him in a manner that is not more general than it at all, saying: ﴿anyone﴾.

When it has become customary that the one being punished is secured by imprisonment or other means, and is prevented from anything by which he could kill himself, out of fear that he might flee or destroy himself, He said: ﴿And none binds as He binds﴾, meaning [none] is found [who binds] His binding, [i.e.] the like of His binding, so how could anyone bind as He binds? The meaning is that, because kinship and means have been cut off, it does not occur to anyone's imagination that anyone could inflict harm of the kind that He, glorified and exalted, is able to inflict, so that one would fear them as one fears in this world. Rather, in this world many illusions occur, that the punishment of those one fears is greater than the punishment of God. And that the entire punishment of this world, even if it were gathered upon one person alone, is not comparable to seeing Hell in that station, in that terrifying assembly, without entering it. For this reason, his fear is placed before the fear of God.

Al-Kisa'i (al-Kisā'ī) and Ya'qub (Ya'qūb) made both verbs passive (yu'adhdhibu and yūthiqu). The meaning, according to the recitation of the majority, which makes them active (for the agent), is: none punishes with a punishment like the punishment of God, i.e., none among the creatures punishes anyone other than God with a punishment like the punishment of God [to him]. The summary is that on the Day of Resurrection he does not fear anyone other than God, for this speech establishes that His punishment has no like. The one being punished is not named, so the matter returns to [the meaning]: ﴿On that Day, man will fear God with a fear that has no like﴾, i.e., he does not fear anyone with a fear like his fear of Him, glorified and exalted. It is also permissible that the pronoun in "ʿadhābihi" (His punishment) refers to man, i.e., none among the guards (al-zabāniyah) punishes anyone other than man with a punishment like his punishment. In the passive reading: none punishes the punishment of man [anyone]. But this is far-fetched, because it would follow that the punishment of man is greater than the punishment of Iblis. It is also permissible that the meaning is: no one bears what he deserves of punishment, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ [Fāṭir: 18].

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 27:

When He knew that this reward mentioned is only for the one who is anxious and distressed (al-halu'), restless of soul, frivolous in times of ease and hardship, who does not honor the orphan or the needy, and who loves this world, and it was known that among people there are those who are not like this, the soul longed for its reward. So He remedied the helplessness of this longing by His saying, to inform that it will be said to their souls at the blowing of the Trumpet (al-Sur) and the scattering of what is in the graves, for resurrection and gathering: ﴿O soul at rest﴾, that is, the one that is in the utmost (p-٤٣) tranquility, with no fear upon it, no grief, no deficiency, and no loss, because it was in this world in the utmost steadfastness upon everything He informed of concerning the Last Abode and other matters, of promise and threat, warning and intimidation. So they hope for His promise and fear His threat. If this is the condition of the soul whose inclination is toward this world, then what is your thought about the spirit which is the best of pure essences?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 89, verse 28:

﴿Return﴾ i.e., by means of resurrection, ﴿to your Lord﴾ i.e., to the appointed time of the One who brought you into being and nurtured you with the upbringing given to those granted success; or to your body, while you are ﴿well-pleased﴾, i.e., with what it is given. There shall reach you no distress in any way at all, just as you were in the abode of anxiety and turmoil [and agitation], tranquil and at rest, submitting to the decree and the divine measure, following the path of contentment, should a trial occur through honour and comfort or through constriction and loss, trusting in what is with Allah. ﴿Well-pleasing﴾ in the sight of Allah and of the rest of His creation. So nothing shall distress you because of what you were, tranquil, doing righteous deeds under the decree and divine measure, its good and its bad, its sweet and its bitter,

Then He explained what had been stated in general about the return, so He said, glory be to Him: ﴿Enter among My servants﴾, that is, by reason of this command, ﴿among My servants﴾, meaning in the company of the righteous who come to Me, those who are worthy of being attributed to Me; or, among the bodies of My servants (p-44) which had departed from them in the world. The reading "ʿabdī" (in the singular) with the definite article for the genus [li-l-jins], encompassing the few and the many, indicates this.

﴿وادْخُلِي جَنَّتِي﴾ [i.e.] and it is Jannat 'Adn (the Garden of Eden), which is the highest of the gardens. Al-Baghawi said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, died [at al-Ta'if], and I attended his funeral. A bird came that we had never seen in its form of creation, and it entered his bier, and we did not see it come out of it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and we did not know who recited it. This latter (verse) is the first of them, according to what is apparent: the one sworn by the dawn, concerning the inevitable resurrection, which, were it not for it, the creation of creatures would be a blameworthy vanity, from which the Living, the Self-Subsisting, is far removed. Glory be to the Greatest King, whose speech this is, its meanings exalted above criticism and its signs made noble, and whose composition and arrangement are firmly set on the peak of inimitability. "And where are the Pleiades from the hand of one who would reach them?"
